decks.title: Locomotion and Movement — Part 1: Movement and muscle contraction
goals: Distinguish amoeboid, ciliary and muscular movement, and movement from locomotion
Compare skeletal, visceral and cardiac muscle
Describe the structure of a skeletal muscle fibre, a sarcomere and the contractile proteins
Explain contraction by the sliding filament theory, and muscle fatigue

slides.heading: Locomotion and Movement
slides.body_md: Part 1 — how cells and muscles move, and how a muscle fibre contracts.

visual.alt: Flow of the three types of movement in human cells and tissues

slides.narration: Movement is one of the significant features of living beings. Some movements, such as walking, running or swimming, change the place of the whole body; these are called locomotion. Cells of the human body show three main types of movement: amoeboid, ciliary and muscular.

slides.heading: Movement and locomotion
slides.body_md: All locomotions are movements, but **all movements are not locomotions**. Methods of locomotion are usually linked to changing habitats and needs, such as finding food, shelter, mates or escaping enemies.

rows: Pseudopodia formed by streaming of protoplasm, with cytoskeletal elements such as microfilaments
Removal of dust in the trachea; passage of ova through the female reproductive tract
Movement of limbs, jaws and tongue

visual.alt: Table of amoeboid, ciliary and muscular movement with examples

slides.narration: Paramecium uses its cilia both to move food into its gullet and to swim, and the tentacles of Hydra catch prey and can also help it move. In our own bodies, white blood cells crawl by pseudopodia, cilia sweep the windpipe clean, and muscles move our limbs.

slides.heading: Three kinds of muscle
slides.body_md: Muscle is a specialised tissue of **mesodermal** origin; about **40 to 50 percent** of an adult’s body weight is muscle. Muscle shows excitability, contractility, extensibility and elasticity.

rows: Inner walls of hollow organs such as the alimentary canal and reproductive tract
Moving food through the gut, gametes through the genital tract

visual.alt: Table comparing skeletal, visceral and cardiac muscle

slides.narration: Skeletal muscles are attached to bones, look striped and work under our will. Visceral muscles line hollow organs such as the gut; they are smooth and involuntary. Cardiac muscle is found only in the heart; its cells join together, it is striated, and it works without our control.

slides.heading: Inside a skeletal muscle
slides.body_md: A skeletal muscle is made of bundles called **fascicles**, held by a collagenous connective tissue layer called **fascia**. Each muscle fibre is lined by the **sarcolemma**; its cytoplasm, the **sarcoplasm**, holds many nuclei (a syncytium), and its endoplasmic reticulum, the **sarcoplasmic reticulum**, is the **store of calcium ions**.

visual.alt: Flow from a whole muscle to fascicles, fibres, myofibrils and sarcomeres

slides.narration: Think of a muscle as a rope of ropes. The muscle is made of fascicles, each fascicle of many muscle fibres, and each fibre is packed with parallel myofibrils. Alternate dark and light bands on the myofibrils give the fibre its striped look.

slides.heading: The sarcomere
slides.body_md: The **light (I) bands** contain **actin** and are **isotropic**; the **dark (A) bands** contain **myosin** and are **anisotropic**. An elastic **Z line** bisects each I band, and the thin filaments are firmly attached to it. The thick filaments in the A band are held together in the middle by a thin **M line**. The part of the A band not overlapped by thin filaments is the **H zone**. The portion between two successive Z lines is the **sarcomere**, the functional unit of contraction.

slides.narration: Each sarcomere runs from one Z line to the next. Thin actin filaments are anchored to the Z lines, and thick myosin filaments sit in the middle, held by the M line. When the muscle contracts, the thin filaments slide inwards, so the I band and the H zone narrow while the A band keeps its length.

slides.heading: Contractile proteins
slides.body_md: Each **actin (thin) filament** is made of two **F (filamentous) actins** helically wound together; each F-actin is a polymer of monomeric **G (globular) actins**. Two filaments of **tropomyosin** run along it, with the complex protein **troponin** at regular intervals. In the resting state, a subunit of troponin **masks the active binding sites for myosin**. Each **myosin (thick) filament** is a polymer of **meromyosin** monomers: a globular head with a short arm (**heavy meromyosin, HMM**) and a tail (**light meromyosin, LMM**). The head is an active **ATPase** with binding sites for ATP and actin.

slides.narration: The thin filament is a twisted double chain of actin beads, with tropomyosin running along it and troponin attached at intervals. The thick filament is a bundle of myosin molecules whose heads stick out as cross arms. Those heads can split ATP and grab actin.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: band widths
slides.body_md: A relaxed sarcomere is 2.5 μm long. Its myosin filaments are 1.6 μm long, and each actin filament reaches 1.0 μm from its Z line. Find the A band, I band and H zone, at rest and after it shortens to 2.1 μm.
bullets: A band = length of the myosin filaments = 1.6 μm, in both states.
Relaxed: I band $= 2.5 - 1.6 = 0.9$ μm; H zone $= 2.5 - 2 \times 1.0 = 0.5$ μm.
Contracted: I band $= 2.1 - 1.6 = 0.5$ μm; H zone $= 2.1 - 2 \times 1.0 = 0.1$ μm.
The A band is unchanged; the I band and H zone shorten because the thin filaments slide over the thick ones.

visual.alt: Worked table of band widths in a relaxed and a contracted sarcomere

slides.narration: The A band is simply the length of the myosin filaments, so it cannot change. The I band is what is left of the sarcomere outside the myosin, and the H zone is the gap between the tips of the two sets of actin filaments. Both shrink as the Z lines are pulled closer. These lengths are typical values chosen for illustration.

slides.heading: How contraction starts
slides.body_md: Contraction is initiated by a signal from the central nervous system through a **motor neuron**. A motor neuron with the muscle fibres it supplies is a **motor unit**; their junction is the **neuromuscular junction (motor end plate)**.

nodes.label: Action potential spreads through the sarcolemma
Ca²⁺ released from the sarcoplasmic reticulum
Ca²⁺ binds a troponin subunit; myosin-binding sites on actin are exposed

visual.alt: Flow from the nerve signal through acetylcholine and calcium release to the unmasking of binding sites

slides.narration: A nerve signal at the motor end plate releases acetylcholine, which sets off an action potential in the sarcolemma. This spreads through the fibre and causes calcium ions to be released from the sarcoplasmic reticulum. Calcium binds to troponin, which removes the mask from the active sites on actin, so myosin can now bind.

slides.heading: Quick check: calcium
slides.body_md: Calcium ions released into the sarcoplasm start contraction by binding to which protein?
slides.narration: Quick check. Which protein masks the binding sites on actin at rest?

slides.heading: The cross-bridge cycle
slides.body_md: Myosin heads, energised by ATP hydrolysis, bind to the exposed sites on actin to form **cross bridges**, and pull the attached actin filaments towards the centre of the A band. The Z lines are pulled inwards, the sarcomere shortens, and the I bands shorten while the A bands keep their length.

nodes.label: Head hydrolyses ATP and is energised
Actin pulled to the A band centre; ADP and Pi released
New ATP binds; cross bridge breaks

visual.alt: Cycle of ATP hydrolysis, cross-bridge formation, pulling and release

slides.narration: The myosin head splits ATP and becomes energised. It binds actin, forming a cross bridge, and pulls the thin filament towards the middle. Releasing ADP and phosphate, the head returns to its relaxed state; a fresh ATP binds and the cross bridge breaks. Repeating this cycle slides the filaments further. When calcium is pumped back into the sarcoplasmic reticulum, the actin sites are masked again and the Z lines return to their original positions.

slides.heading: Fatigue, red and white fibres
slides.body_md: Repeated activation of muscles can lead to accumulation of **lactic acid** from the anaerobic breakdown of glycogen, causing **fatigue**.

visual.alt: Table comparing red and white muscle fibres

slides.narration: Red fibres are packed with myoglobin and mitochondria, so they use the stored oxygen for steady aerobic work. White fibres are pale, with few mitochondria but plenty of sarcoplasmic reticulum, and rely on anaerobic energy. Hard repeated work makes lactic acid build up, and the muscle tires.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: shortening a myofibril
slides.body_md: A myofibril has 4000 sarcomeres in series, each 2.5 μm long at rest. During a contraction each shortens to 2.1 μm. Find the myofibril’s length before and after, and the percentage shortening.
bullets: Before: $4000 \times 2.5 = 10000$ μm, which is 10 mm.
After: $4000 \times 2.1 = 8400$ μm, which is 8.4 mm.
Shortening: $4000 \times 0.4 = 1600$ μm, or 1.6 mm; percentage $= \dfrac{0.4}{2.5} \times 100 = 16$.
Tiny shortenings of thousands of sarcomeres in series add up to a visible movement.

visual.alt: Worked table: a myofibril of 4000 sarcomeres shortens by 1.6 mm

slides.narration: Each sarcomere shortens by less than half a micrometre, far too little to see. But four thousand of them in a row shorten the whole myofibril by more than a millimetre and a half, the same fraction, sixteen percent, as each single sarcomere.

slides.heading: Quick check: the A band
slides.body_md: Judge the assertion and the reason about the A band during contraction.
slides.narration: Quick check. Do the myosin filaments themselves get shorter?

slides.heading: Summary
bullets: Movements: amoeboid (macrophages, leucocytes), ciliary (trachea, oviduct), muscular (limbs, jaws, tongue); locomotion changes the place of the body.
Muscle: skeletal (striated, voluntary), visceral (smooth, involuntary), cardiac (striated, involuntary).
Muscle → fascicles → fibres (sarcolemma, sarcoplasm, sarcoplasmic reticulum storing Ca²⁺) → myofibrils → sarcomeres.
I band: actin, isotropic; A band: myosin, anisotropic; Z line, M line, H zone; sarcomere between two Z lines.
Nerve signal → acetylcholine → action potential → Ca²⁺ → troponin → cross bridges (ATP) → actin slides; I band and H zone shorten, A band constant.
Fatigue: lactic acid; red fibres aerobic (myoglobin, mitochondria), white fibres anaerobic.

visual.alt: Summary table of band changes during contraction

slides.narration: To recap: cells move by pseudopodia, cilia or muscles. A muscle fibre is a chain of sarcomeres. A nerve signal releases calcium, calcium frees the binding sites on actin, and myosin heads powered by ATP pull the thin filaments inwards. The A band stays the same while the I band and H zone shrink.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: Draw a **labelled sarcomere**: Z line, M line, A band, I band, H zone, actin and myosin.
Write the **sequence** from the motor neuron to the power stroke in order.
State which bands **shorten** and which **stays constant**.
Give the roles of **troponin**, **tropomyosin**, **calcium** and **ATP**.
slides.narration: Exam tips. Practise drawing and labelling a sarcomere. Learn the steps of contraction in order, from the nerve signal to the sliding of actin. Remember that the A band stays constant. And be ready to explain the roles of calcium, troponin and ATP.

slides.heading: Skeletal system and joints
slides.body_md: Part 2 — the framework of bones and cartilages, the joints that let it move, and what can go wrong.

visual.alt: Flow from the axial and appendicular skeleton to joints and disorders

slides.narration: The skeletal system is a framework of bones and a few cartilages. Bone has a very hard matrix because of calcium salts, while cartilage has a slightly pliable matrix because of chondroitin salts. Together with muscles, the skeleton makes movement possible.

slides.heading: Two divisions: 206 bones

slides.narration: The axial skeleton runs along the main axis of the body: the skull, the vertebral column, the sternum and the ribs. The appendicular skeleton is made of the bones of the limbs and the girdles that attach them to the axial skeleton.

slides.heading: The skull
slides.body_md: The skull has **8 cranial bones**, forming the hard protective cranium around the brain, and **14 facial bones**, forming the front part of the skull. A single U-shaped **hyoid** bone lies at the base of the buccal cavity, and each middle ear has **three tiny ear ossicles**: malleus, incus and stapes. The skull articulates with the vertebral column by **two occipital condyles** (a **dicondylic** skull).

visual.alt: Table of the bones of the skull region

slides.narration: Eight cranial bones form a strong box around the brain and fourteen bones shape the face. Add the small hyoid bone in the floor of the mouth and three ossicles in each middle ear, and the skull region has twenty nine bones.

slides.heading: Vertebral column and ribs
slides.body_md: The **vertebral column** has **26 serially arranged vertebrae** and is dorsally placed. Each vertebra has a central hollow, the **neural canal**, through which the spinal cord passes. The first vertebra is the **atlas**, which articulates with the occipital condyles. The column protects the spinal cord, supports the head and serves as the point of attachment for the ribs and musculature of the back. The **sternum** is a flat bone on the ventral midline of the thorax. There are **12 pairs of ribs**; each rib is a thin flat bone joined dorsally to the vertebral column and ventrally (in most) to the sternum, with two articulation surfaces on its dorsal end (**bicephalic**).

slides.body_md: Each limb has 30 bones. The **pectoral girdle** (a clavicle and a scapula on each side) and the **pelvic girdle** (two coxal bones) attach the limbs to the axial skeleton.

slides.narration: Joints are classified by how much movement they allow. Fibrous joints, such as the sutures between flat skull bones, allow none. Cartilaginous joints, such as those between neighbouring vertebrae, allow a little. Synovial joints have a fluid-filled cavity between the bones and allow considerable movement.

slides.heading: Five kinds of synovial joint
slides.body_md: Synovial joints are characterised by a fluid-filled **synovial cavity** between the articulating surfaces of the two bones. They allow considerable movement and play a significant role in locomotion and many other movements.

rows: Between the humerus and the pectoral girdle
Between the atlas and the axis
Between the carpal and metacarpal of the thumb

visual.alt: Table of five kinds of synovial joint with examples

slides.narration: A ball and socket joint, as at the shoulder, lets the arm move in almost every direction. A hinge, as at the knee, works in one plane like a door. A pivot lets the head turn on the neck. Gliding joints let small bones slide over each other, and a saddle joint gives the thumb its wide range.

slides.body_md: Some disorders affect the junction between nerve and muscle, some the muscle itself, and some the bones and joints.

rows: Autoimmune disorder affecting the neuromuscular junction: fatigue, weakening and paralysis of skeletal muscle
Progressive degeneration of skeletal muscle, mostly due to a genetic disorder
Rapid spasms (wild contractions) in muscle due to low Ca²⁺ in body fluid
Age-related disorder: decreased bone mass and increased chances of fractures; decreased levels of oestrogen is a common cause
Inflammation of joints due to accumulation of uric acid crystals

visual.alt: Table of six disorders of the muscular and skeletal systems

slides.narration: In myasthenia gravis the body attacks its own neuromuscular junctions, so muscles weaken. Muscular dystrophy is an inherited, steady wasting of muscle. Too little calcium in body fluids causes the spasms of tetany. Arthritis inflames joints, gout does so through uric acid crystals, and osteoporosis thins the bones with age.

slides.heading: Summary
bullets: 206 bones: axial 80 (skull 29, vertebrae 26, sternum 1, ribs 24) and appendicular 126 (limbs 120, girdles 6).
Vertebrae: cervical 7, thoracic 12, lumbar 5, sacral 1, coccygeal 1; atlas articulates with the occipital condyles.
Ribs: true 1–7, false (vertebrochondral) 8–10, floating 11–12.
Joints: fibrous (skull sutures), cartilaginous (vertebrae), synovial (ball and socket, hinge, pivot, gliding, saddle).
Disorders: myasthenia gravis, muscular dystrophy, tetany, arthritis, osteoporosis, gout.

slides.narration: To recap: the skeleton has two hundred and six bones, eighty axial and one hundred and twenty six appendicular. Joints range from fixed sutures to freely moving synovial joints. And disorders can strike the neuromuscular junction, the muscle, the bone or the joint.

notes.title: Locomotion and Movement — Notes

sections.heading: 1. Types of movement; muscle structure and contraction
sections.body_md:
**Movement** is a significant feature of living beings. Voluntary movements that result in a change of place or location are **locomotion** (walking, running, climbing, flying, swimming). All locomotions are movements, but all movements are not locomotions. In *Paramecium*, cilia move food through the cytopharynx and also help in locomotion; *Hydra* uses its tentacles to capture prey and to move.

**Types of movement in human cells**
- **Amoeboid:** macrophages and leucocytes in blood move by **pseudopodia**, formed by streaming of protoplasm (as in *Amoeba*); cytoskeletal elements such as microfilaments are involved.
- **Ciliary:** occurs in internal tubular organs lined by ciliated epithelium; coordinated beating of cilia in the **trachea** removes dust particles and foreign substances inhaled with air, and passage of **ova** through the female reproductive tract is helped by ciliary movement.
- **Muscular:** movement of limbs, jaws and tongue needs muscular movement; locomotion needs the coordinated activity of the muscular, skeletal and neural systems.

**Muscle** is a specialised tissue of **mesodermal** origin forming about **40–50 percent** of an adult’s body weight; it shows excitability, contractility, extensibility and elasticity.
- **Skeletal** muscles are attached to bones, striated and voluntary; they help in locomotion and changes of body posture.
- **Visceral** muscles lie in the inner walls of hollow visceral organs (alimentary canal, reproductive tract); they are smooth (non-striated) and involuntary, and help, for example, in moving food through the digestive tract and gametes through the genital tract.
- **Cardiac** muscles form the heart; many cells assemble in a branching pattern; they are striated and involuntary.

**Structure of a skeletal muscle.** A muscle is made of bundles called **fascicles**, held together by a collagenous connective tissue layer, the **fascia**. Each **muscle fibre** is lined by the plasma membrane (**sarcolemma**) around the **sarcoplasm**; the fibre is a **syncytium** (many nuclei). The endoplasmic reticulum, the **sarcoplasmic reticulum**, is the **store of calcium ions**. Many parallel **myofibrils** (myofilaments) in the sarcoplasm show alternate dark and light bands: the **light I band** contains **actin** and is **isotropic**; the **dark A band** contains **myosin** and is **anisotropic**. An elastic **Z line** bisects each I band; thin filaments are firmly attached to it. Thick filaments in the A band are held together in the middle by the thin **M line**. The central part of the A band not overlapped by thin filaments is the **H zone**. The portion of the myofibril between two successive Z lines is a **sarcomere**, the functional unit of contraction.

**Contractile proteins.** Each actin (thin) filament is made of two **F (filamentous) actins** helically wound; each F-actin is a polymer of **G (globular) actins**. Two filaments of **tropomyosin** run close to the F-actins along their length, and the complex protein **troponin** is distributed at regular intervals; in the resting state a subunit of troponin **masks the active binding sites for myosin**. Each myosin (thick) filament is a polymerised protein; its monomer, **meromyosin**, has a globular **head with a short arm** (**heavy meromyosin, HMM**) and a **tail** (**light meromyosin, LMM**). The HMM projects outwards from the filament as a **cross arm**; the globular head is an active **ATPase** with binding sites for ATP and active sites for actin.

**Mechanism: the sliding filament theory.** Contraction of a muscle fibre takes place by the sliding of the thin filaments over the thick filaments.
1. A signal from the CNS via a **motor neuron** reaches the **neuromuscular junction** (motor end plate); a motor neuron with the fibres it supplies is a **motor unit**.
2. **Acetylcholine** released there generates an **action potential** in the sarcolemma, which spreads through the fibre.
3. **Calcium ions** are released from the sarcoplasmic reticulum into the sarcoplasm.
4. Ca²⁺ binds to a subunit of **troponin** on the actin filaments, removing the masking of the active sites for myosin.
5. Using energy from **ATP hydrolysis**, the myosin head binds to the exposed sites on actin to form a **cross bridge**, which pulls the attached actin filaments towards the centre of the **A band**. The Z lines are pulled inwards and the sarcomere shortens (contraction). The **I bands shorten**, the **H zone narrows**, and the **A band keeps its length**.
6. The myosin, releasing ADP and Pi, goes back to its relaxed state; a new ATP binds and the cross bridge is broken. The cycle of cross-bridge formation and breakage repeats, causing further sliding.
7. The process continues until Ca²⁺ ions are pumped back into the sarcoplasmic cisternae, which again masks the actin filaments; the Z lines return to their original position (**relaxation**).

With illustrative lengths, a 2.5 μm sarcomere with a 1.6 μm A band has an I band of 0.9 μm and an H zone of 0.5 μm; at 2.1 μm these become 0.5 μm and 0.1 μm, while the A band stays 1.6 μm.

**Fatigue.** Repeated activation of muscles can lead to accumulation of **lactic acid** from the anaerobic breakdown of glycogen, causing fatigue. **Red fibres** contain plenty of the red, oxygen-storing pigment **myoglobin** and many mitochondria, and are called **aerobic muscles**. **White fibres** have very little myoglobin and fewer mitochondria but a large amount of sarcoplasmic reticulum, and depend on anaerobic processes for energy.

sections.heading: 2. Skeletal system and joints
sections.body_md:
The skeletal system is a framework of **bones** and a few **cartilages**. Bone has a very hard matrix due to **calcium salts**; cartilage has a slightly pliable matrix due to **chondroitin salts**. In human beings the skeletal system has **206 bones**, grouped into the **axial skeleton (80 bones)** and the **appendicular skeleton (126 bones)**.

**Axial skeleton** — skull, vertebral column, sternum and ribs.
- **Skull:** 8 **cranial** bones forming the hard protective cranium, and 14 **facial** bones forming the front part; a single U-shaped **hyoid** bone at the base of the buccal cavity and three **ear ossicles** (malleus, incus, stapes) in each middle ear are included in the skull region (29 bones). The skull joins the vertebral column through **two occipital condyles** (dicondylic skull).
- **Vertebral column:** 26 serially arranged vertebrae, dorsally placed: **cervical 7, thoracic 12, lumbar 5, sacral 1 (fused), coccygeal 1 (fused)**. Each vertebra has a central **neural canal** through which the spinal cord passes. The first vertebra, the **atlas**, articulates with the occipital condyles. The number of cervical vertebrae is seven in almost all mammals, including humans. The column protects the spinal cord, supports the head and gives attachment to the ribs and back muscles.
- **Sternum:** a flat bone on the ventral midline of the thorax.
- **Ribs:** 12 pairs; each is a thin flat bone joined dorsally to the vertebral column and ventrally to the sternum, with two articulation surfaces on its dorsal end (**bicephalic**). The first seven pairs are **true ribs**, attached ventrally to the sternum by hyaline cartilage; the **8th, 9th and 10th** pairs do not join the sternum directly but join the seventh rib by hyaline cartilage (**vertebrochondral** or false ribs); the **11th and 12th** pairs are not connected ventrally (**floating ribs**). Thoracic vertebrae, ribs and sternum together form the **rib cage**.

**Appendicular skeleton** — limbs and girdles.
- **Fore limb (hand):** humerus, radius and ulna, 8 **carpals** (wrist), 5 **metacarpals** (palm) and 14 **phalanges** (digits) — 30 bones.
- **Hind limb (leg):** **femur** (thigh bone, the longest bone), tibia and fibula, 7 **tarsals** (ankle), 5 **metatarsals** and 14 phalanges, and a cup-shaped **patella** covering the knee ventrally (knee cap) — 30 bones.
- **Pectoral girdle:** each half has a **clavicle** (collar bone) and a **scapula**; the scapula, a large triangular flat bone in the dorsal part of the thorax between the second and seventh ribs, has a flat projection, the **acromion**, which articulates with the clavicle, and below it a depression, the **glenoid cavity**, which articulates with the head of the humerus to form the shoulder joint.
- **Pelvic girdle:** two **coxal** bones, each formed by fusion of the **ilium, ischium and pubis**; at their point of fusion is a cavity, the **acetabulum**, to which the thigh bone articulates. The two halves meet ventrally to form the **pubic symphysis** (fibrous cartilage).

**Joints** are points of contact between bones, or between bones and cartilages. Force generated by the muscles is used to carry out movement through joints, where the joint acts as a **fulcrum**.
- **Fibrous joints** do not allow any movement; flat skull bones fuse end to end with dense fibrous connective tissue as **sutures** to form the cranium.
- **Cartilaginous joints** have the bones joined together with cartilage and permit **limited** movement, for example between adjacent vertebrae.
- **Synovial joints** have a fluid-filled **synovial cavity** between the articulating surfaces and allow **considerable** movement: **ball and socket** (humerus and pectoral girdle), **hinge** (knee joint), **pivot** (atlas and axis), **gliding** (between the carpals), **saddle** (carpal and metacarpal of the thumb).

sections.heading: 3. Disorders of the muscular and skeletal systems
sections.body_md:
- **Myasthenia gravis:** an **autoimmune** disorder affecting the **neuromuscular junction**, leading to fatigue, weakening and paralysis of skeletal muscle.
- **Muscular dystrophy:** progressive **degeneration of skeletal muscle**, mostly due to a **genetic** disorder.
- **Tetany:** rapid spasms (wild contractions) in muscle due to **low Ca²⁺** in body fluid.
- **Arthritis:** **inflammation of joints**.
- **Osteoporosis:** an **age-related** disorder characterised by **decreased bone mass** and increased chances of **fractures**; **decreased levels of oestrogen** is a common cause.
- **Gout:** inflammation of joints due to accumulation of **uric acid crystals**.

key_terms.definition_md: Autoimmune disorder of the neuromuscular junction causing fatigue, weakness and paralysis of skeletal muscle.
Rapid spasms in muscle due to low Ca²⁺ in body fluid.
Age-related loss of bone mass with more fractures; low oestrogen is a common cause.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Writing that the A band shortens during contraction (it stays constant; the I band and H zone shorten).
- Putting actin in the A band only or myosin in the I band (the I band has only actin; the A band has myosin, overlapped by actin except in the H zone).
- Saying calcium binds to tropomyosin or to myosin (it binds to a subunit of troponin).
- Saying ATP is needed only to form cross bridges (a new ATP is also needed to break the cross bridge).
- Counting the hyoid and ear ossicles outside the skull region, or forgetting the patella in the hind limb.
- Calling ribs 8–10 floating ribs (they are false, vertebrochondral ribs; 11–12 are floating).
- Mixing up gout (uric acid) and tetany (low Ca²⁺).

**How marks are usually awarded**
- 1-mark items: name a band, a protein, a joint, a bone or a disorder.
- 2–3-mark answers: types of muscle; red and white fibres; actin or myosin structure; kinds of ribs; joints with examples; disorders.
- 5-mark answers: sliding filament theory with a labelled sarcomere; the axial and appendicular skeleton with counts; joints.
- Case-based items: sarcomere measurements, fibre types and fatigue, an injured joint, or clinic cases of disorders, with a 2-mark part with an internal choice.

questions.stem_md: In a cut on a child’s knee, certain white blood cells crawl out of the capillaries towards invading bacteria by pushing out temporary projections of their cytoplasm. Which type of movement is this?
questions.solution_md: Macrophages and leucocytes move by pseudopodia formed by streaming of protoplasm, as in Amoeba — option (a).

questions.stem_md: Fine soot inhaled by a traffic policeman is trapped in mucus and carried up the windpipe towards the throat. Which kind of movement clears it?

options.text_md: Amoeboid movement of the tracheal cells
Coordinated beating of cilia lining the trachea
Voluntary contraction of skeletal muscle in the trachea

questions.solution_md: Coordinated movement of cilia in the trachea removes dust particles and foreign substances inhaled with the atmospheric air — option (b).

questions.stem_md: Smooth, involuntary muscles located in the inner walls of hollow organs such as the alimentary canal are called
questions.solution_md: Visceral muscles line the inner walls of hollow visceral organs; they are smooth and involuntary — option (d).

questions.stem_md: Which combination of features describes cardiac muscle?

options.text_md: Striated, involuntary, cells assembled in a branching pattern
Smooth, involuntary, found in the walls of the gut

questions.solution_md: Cardiac muscle cells assemble in a branching pattern; the muscle is striated and involuntary — option (b).

questions.stem_md: The endoplasmic reticulum of a muscle fibre, which stores calcium ions, is known as the
questions.solution_md: The sarcoplasmic reticulum is the store of calcium ions; the sarcolemma is the plasma membrane and the fascia binds fascicles — option (c).

questions.stem_md: The light band of a myofibril, which is isotropic, contains
questions.solution_md: The light (I) band contains actin and is isotropic; the dark (A) band contains myosin and is anisotropic — option (b).

questions.stem_md: Calcium ions released into the sarcoplasm during excitation of a muscle fibre bind to

options.text_md: a subunit of troponin on the actin filaments
the M line of the A band

questions.solution_md: Calcium binds with a subunit of troponin on the actin filaments and thereby removes the masking of the active sites for myosin — option (c).

questions.stem_md: In a resting skeletal muscle fibre, myosin heads cannot attach to the thin filaments because

options.text_md: the myosin heads have no ATPase activity at rest
actin filaments are absent from the I band at rest
the sarcoplasmic reticulum holds the myosin filaments
a subunit of troponin masks the active binding sites for myosin on actin

questions.solution_md: In the resting state a subunit of troponin masks the active binding sites for myosin on the actin filaments — option (d).

questions.stem_md: Which part of a myosin monomer (meromyosin) acts as an ATPase and carries the binding site for actin?

options.text_md: The globular head of heavy meromyosin

questions.solution_md: The globular head with its short arm is heavy meromyosin (HMM); the head is an active ATPase with binding sites for ATP and actin — option (b).

questions.stem_md: A snake venom blocks the receptors for acetylcholine on the sarcolemma at the motor end plate. What is the most likely immediate effect on the prey’s skeletal muscles?

options.text_md: The muscles contract continuously because calcium is released without stopping.
The muscles switch from aerobic to anaerobic respiration only.
Nerve signals fail to set off action potentials in the muscle fibres, so the muscles cannot contract.
The A bands of the sarcomeres shorten.

questions.solution_md: Acetylcholine at the neuromuscular junction generates the action potential in the sarcolemma; with its receptors blocked, the signal does not pass and the fibres do not contract — option (c).

questions.stem_md: The breast muscles of a migratory goose keep working for many hours of continuous flight. Their fibres are most likely to be rich in

options.text_md: sarcoplasmic reticulum, with very little myoglobin (white fibres)

questions.solution_md: Sustained aerobic work needs red fibres, with plenty of myoglobin to store oxygen and many mitochondria — option (a).

questions.stem_md: After a 400-metre race run at full speed, a student’s thigh muscles feel heavy and tired. Which substance has most probably built up in them?

options.text_md: Lactic acid from the anaerobic breakdown of glycogen

questions.solution_md: Repeated activation of muscles can lead to accumulation of lactic acid from anaerobic breakdown of glycogen, causing fatigue — option (b).

questions.stem_md: In an experiment, isolated muscle fibres are allowed to use up all their ATP. Their myosin heads are then found locked onto the actin filaments. Which step of the contraction cycle has been blocked?

options.text_md: Breaking of the cross bridge, which needs a new ATP to bind to the myosin head
Release of calcium from the sarcoplasmic reticulum
Binding of acetylcholine to the sarcolemma

questions.solution_md: Myosin releases ADP and Pi and a new ATP binds, breaking the cross bridge; without ATP the heads stay attached — option (a).

questions.stem_md: An electron micrograph of a strongly contracted fibre shows that the H zone can no longer be seen, although the A band has its usual width. What best explains this?

options.text_md: The myosin filaments have shortened to half their length.
The actin filaments have been converted into myosin.
The thin filaments from both ends have slid inwards until they meet at the centre of the A band.

questions.solution_md: The H zone is the part of the A band not overlapped by thin filaments; when the thin filaments slide right in, it disappears while the A band (myosin length) is unchanged — option (d).

questions.stem_md: Which ribs are called floating ribs?

options.text_md: The 11th and 12th pairs, which are not connected ventrally
The 8th, 9th and 10th pairs, which join the seventh rib by cartilage
The first seven pairs, which join the sternum directly
All ribs attached to the lumbar vertebrae

questions.solution_md: The last two pairs (11th and 12th) are not connected ventrally and are called floating ribs — option (a).

questions.stem_md: The first vertebra, which articulates with the occipital condyles of the skull, is the
questions.solution_md: The first vertebra is the atlas, and it articulates with the occipital condyles — option (a).

questions.stem_md: The joint between the atlas and the axis is a
questions.solution_md: The atlas–axis joint is the standard example of a pivot joint — option (d).

questions.stem_md: A rock climber’s thumb can be swung across the palm and also tilted in a wide arc, which no finger can do. Which joint makes this possible?

options.text_md: A pivot joint between the atlas and the axis
A fibrous joint between the carpals
A cartilaginous joint between the phalanges
A saddle joint between the carpal and metacarpal of the thumb

questions.solution_md: The joint between the carpal and metacarpal of the thumb is a saddle joint — option (d).

questions.stem_md: A football player can bend and straighten her knee freely but cannot twist her lower leg round in a circle at the knee. What type of joint is the knee?
questions.solution_md: The knee is a hinge joint, allowing movement mainly in one plane — option (d).

questions.stem_md: A fast bowler whirls his arm through a complete circle at the shoulder during his run-up. Which joint allows this, and between which bones?

options.text_md: Hinge joint, between the humerus and the ulna
Saddle joint, between the clavicle and the sternum
Ball and socket joint, between the humerus and the pectoral girdle
Pivot joint, between the scapula and the ribs

questions.solution_md: The head of the humerus fits the glenoid cavity of the scapula: a ball and socket joint between the humerus and the pectoral girdle — option (c).

questions.stem_md: The joints between adjacent vertebrae, where the bones are joined by cartilage, allow

options.text_md: considerable movement through a synovial cavity

questions.solution_md: Cartilaginous joints, such as those between adjacent vertebrae, permit limited movement — option (c).

questions.stem_md: Flat bones of the cranium fuse end to end with dense fibrous connective tissue. These sutures are an example of

options.text_md: synovial joints that allow free movement
cartilaginous joints that allow limited movement
fibrous joints that allow no movement

questions.solution_md: Fibrous joints do not allow any movement; the skull sutures are the example — option (c).

questions.stem_md: Explain the sliding filament theory of muscle contraction. Describe the events from the nerve signal to relaxation, and state how each band of the sarcomere changes.

answer.model_answer_md:
According to the **sliding filament theory**, a muscle fibre contracts because the **thin (actin) filaments slide over the thick (myosin) filaments**; neither set of filaments shortens.

**Excitation.** A signal from the central nervous system reaches the **neuromuscular junction** through a **motor neuron**, which releases **acetylcholine**. This generates an **action potential** in the **sarcolemma** that spreads through the fibre and causes the release of **Ca²⁺** from the **sarcoplasmic reticulum**.

**Cross-bridge cycle.** Ca²⁺ binds a subunit of **troponin**, removing the masking of the active sites on actin. The myosin head, energised by **hydrolysing ATP**, binds the exposed site to form a **cross bridge** and pulls the actin filament towards the centre of the **A band**. Releasing ADP and Pi, the head relaxes; a **new ATP** binds and the cross bridge breaks. Repeated cycles cause further sliding.

**Band changes.** The **Z lines** are pulled inwards, so the **sarcomere shortens**; the **I bands shorten**, the **H zone narrows or disappears**, but the **A band keeps its length**.

**Relaxation.** Ca²⁺ is pumped back into the sarcoplasmic reticulum, the actin sites are masked again, and the Z lines return to their original positions.

questions.solution_md: Theory, excitation, cross bridges, bands, relaxation.

questions.stem_md: Describe the structure of a skeletal muscle, from the whole muscle to its contractile proteins. Explain why its fibres appear striated.

answer.model_answer_md:
**Muscle to fibre.** A skeletal muscle is made of bundles called **fascicles**, held together by a collagenous connective tissue layer, the **fascia**. Each fascicle contains many **muscle fibres**. A fibre is lined by the **sarcolemma** around the **sarcoplasm**, which has many nuclei (a **syncytium**). Its endoplasmic reticulum, the **sarcoplasmic reticulum**, stores **calcium ions**.

**Myofibrils and striations.** Many parallel **myofibrils** fill the sarcoplasm. They show alternate **light I bands**, containing **actin** (isotropic), and **dark A bands**, containing **myosin** (anisotropic). This regular pattern of actin and myosin gives the **striated** appearance. An elastic **Z line** bisects each I band; an **M line** holds the thick filaments in the middle of the A band; the **H zone** is the part of the A band not overlapped by thin filaments. The unit between two Z lines is the **sarcomere**.

**Contractile proteins.** Each thin filament has **two F-actins**, polymers of **G-actin**, helically wound, with **tropomyosin** along them and **troponin** at intervals; a troponin subunit masks myosin-binding sites at rest. Each thick filament is a polymer of **meromyosin**: a globular **heavy meromyosin** head with a short arm, projecting as a **cross arm**, and a **light meromyosin** tail. The head is an **ATPase** with binding sites for ATP and actin.

questions.solution_md: Levels of organisation, bands, proteins.

marking_scheme.step: Fascicles, fibre, sarcolemma, sarcoplasm, sarcoplasmic reticulum
Bands, lines, H zone, sarcomere, striation

questions.stem_md: Describe the human axial and appendicular skeleton, giving the number of bones in each part.

answer.model_answer_md:
The human skeleton has **206 bones**: **80 axial** and **126 appendicular**.

**Axial skeleton.** The **skull region (29)** has 8 cranial bones forming the protective cranium, 14 facial bones, the U-shaped **hyoid** at the base of the buccal cavity and 3 **ear ossicles** in each middle ear; it joins the vertebral column by two occipital condyles (dicondylic). The **vertebral column (26)** has cervical 7, thoracic 12, lumbar 5, sacral 1 and coccygeal 1 vertebrae; the first, the **atlas**, articulates with the occipital condyles, and each vertebra has a **neural canal** for the spinal cord. The **sternum (1)** is a flat ventral bone. There are **12 pairs of ribs (24)**: true ribs 1–7, false ribs 8–10, floating ribs 11–12. Thoracic vertebrae, ribs and sternum form the **rib cage**.

**Appendicular skeleton.** Each **fore limb (30)** has the humerus, radius, ulna, 8 carpals, 5 metacarpals and 14 phalanges. Each **hind limb (30)** has the femur, tibia, fibula, 7 tarsals, 5 metatarsals, 14 phalanges and the patella. The **pectoral girdle** has a clavicle and a scapula on each side; the glenoid cavity of the scapula takes the humerus. The **pelvic girdle** has two **coxal bones**, each of fused ilium, ischium and pubis, with an **acetabulum** for the femur; they meet at the **pubic symphysis**.

questions.stem_md: A physiotherapist examining a gymnast checks the skull sutures, the spine, the shoulder, the knee, the neck rotation, the wrist and the thumb. Classify the joints at each of these places, and explain how the structure of each class of joint determines the movement it allows.

answer.model_answer_md:
**Fibrous joints — skull sutures.** The flat cranial bones are fused end to end by dense **fibrous connective tissue**, so **no movement** is possible; this protects the brain.

**Cartilaginous joints — the spine.** Adjacent **vertebrae** are joined by **cartilage**, which allows only **limited** bending, so the column is flexible yet protects the spinal cord.

**Synovial joints** have a fluid-filled **synovial cavity** between the articulating surfaces, permitting **considerable movement**:
- **Shoulder:** **ball and socket** joint between the humerus and the pectoral girdle; movement in many directions.
- **Knee:** **hinge** joint; movement mainly in one plane.
- **Neck rotation:** **pivot** joint between the **atlas and axis**, letting the head turn.
- **Wrist:** **gliding** joints between the carpals; small sliding movements.
- **Thumb:** **saddle** joint between the carpal and metacarpal; a wide range of movement.

In every case the joint acts as a **fulcrum** through which the force of muscle contraction produces movement.

questions.solution_md: Classify and relate structure to movement.

questions.stem_md: A coach claims: “A marathon runner and a 100-metre sprinter need exactly the same kind of muscle fibres, and both tire for the same reason.” Evaluate this claim using your knowledge of red and white fibres, the energy needs of contraction and muscle fatigue.

answer.model_answer_md:
**Shared basis.** In both athletes contraction works the same way: Ca²⁺ released from the sarcoplasmic reticulum unmasks actin, and myosin heads use **ATP** to form and break **cross bridges**. So both need a steady supply of ATP.

**Different fibres.** A **marathon** lasts hours and needs ATP made **aerobically**. This suits **red fibres**, rich in the oxygen-storing pigment **myoglobin** and in **mitochondria**; they are called aerobic muscles. A **sprint** lasts seconds and needs very rapid, powerful contraction. **White fibres**, with little myoglobin and few mitochondria but much **sarcoplasmic reticulum**, depend on **anaerobic** processes and suit such bursts.

**Fatigue.** In the sprinter, intense repeated activation drives **anaerobic breakdown of glycogen**, and **lactic acid** accumulates quickly, causing fatigue. The marathon runner works mostly aerobically, so lactic acid builds up far more slowly; tiredness comes much later and has other contributing causes.

**Judgement.** The claim is **only partly correct**. The contraction mechanism is the same, but the two events favour **different fibre types**, and fatigue does not arise in the same way or at the same rate.

children.stem_md: **Either** (i): Name the type of joint at the shoulder and explain why a joint that allows so much movement can also be dislocated quite easily.

answer.model_answer_md: It is a **ball and socket** synovial joint between the humerus and the pectoral girdle. The **rounded head** sits in a **shallow cavity**, giving movement in **many directions**; the same shallow fit means a strong force can push the head out of the socket.

alternatives.stem_md: **Or** (ii): Describe the features of the synovial joint found at the fielder’s shoulder that allow smooth movement.

answer.model_answer_md: A synovial joint has a fluid-filled **synovial cavity** between the articulating surfaces of the bones. The bone ends are covered by smooth cartilage, and the joint is enclosed by a capsule, so the bones move **freely and smoothly**, allowing **considerable movement**.

questions.passage_md:
Three patients visited an orthopaedic clinic on the same morning.

- **Patient P**, 35, had sudden, painful cramps of the hand muscles; her blood calcium level was well below normal.
- **Patient Q**, 58, had a red, swollen, very painful joint at the base of his big toe; his blood uric acid level was high.
- **Patient R**, 70, a woman long past menopause, had broken a vertebra while lifting a bucket; a scan showed low bone mass.

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** (d) tetany

**(b)** (b) gout, the accumulation of uric acid crystals in the joint

**(c)** (i) Patient R has **osteoporosis**, an age-related disorder with **decreased bone mass** and increased chances of **fractures**. After menopause the level of **oestrogen falls**, and decreased oestrogen is a common cause, so older women are especially at risk.

**OR** (ii) He has **myasthenia gravis**, an **autoimmune** disorder affecting the **neuromuscular junction**. Signals from motor neurons are not passed on properly to the muscle fibres, so the muscles show **fatigue, weakening** and, in severe cases, **paralysis**.
